questions.question:
A parallel plate capacitor made of circular plates is being charged such that the surface charge density on its plates is increasing at a constant rate with time. The magnetic field arising due to displacement current is:
1. non-zero everywhere with a maximum at the imaginary cylindrical surface connecting the peripheries of the plates.
2. zero between the plates and non-zero outside.
3. zero at all places.
4. constant between the plates and zero outside the plates.
questions.explanation:
Hint: Use the concept of displacement current in a charging capacitor and apply Ampere-Maxwell law.

Explanation: As the surface charge density on the plates of a parallel plate capacitor increases at a constant rate, there is a changing electric field between the plates, which gives rise to a displacement current. According to Maxwell’s modification of Ampere’s law, this displacement current produces a magnetic field that forms concentric circles around the axis, similar to the magnetic field around a conduction current. The magnetic field is zero outside the plates, because outside the plates the electric field is nearly zero, so no displacement current flows there. Between the plates, the magnetic field is non-zero and increases with radial distance from the axis, reaching its maximum near the edge of the imaginary cylindrical surface connecting the peripheries of the plates.
Hence, option (1) is the correct answer.

questions.question:
An electric dipole with dipole moment \(5\times10^{-6}~\text{C-m} \) is aligned with the direction of a uniform electric field of magnitude \(4\times10^{5}~\text{N/C}. \) The dipole is then rotated through an angle of \(60^\circ\) with respect to the electric field. The change in the potential energy of the dipole is:
1. \(1.2~\text{J}\) 2. \(1.5~\text{J}\)
3. \(0.8~\text{J}\) 4. \(1.0~\text{J}\)
questions.explanation:
Hint: \(U=-pE\cos\theta\)

Step: Find the change in the potential energy of the dipole.
\(\Delta U=U_2-U_1 \)
\(\Rightarrow \Delta U=-pE\cos\theta_2-(-pE\cos\theta_1) \)
\(\Rightarrow \Delta U=pE(\cos\theta_1-\cos\theta_2)\)
\(\Rightarrow \Delta U=5\times10^{-6}\times4\times10^{5}(\cos0^{\circ}-\cos60^{\circ})\)
\(\Rightarrow \Delta U=1.0~\text{J}\)
Hence, option (4) is the correct answer.

questions.question:
Three identical heat conducting rods are connected in series as shown in the figure. The rods on the sides have thermal conductivity \(2K\) while that in the middle has thermal conductivity \(K\). The left end of the combination is maintained at temperature \(3T\) and the right end at \(T.\) The rods are thermally insulated from outside. In the steady state, temperature at the left junction is \(T_1\) and that at the right junction is \(T_2\). The ratio \(\dfrac{T_1}{T_2}\) is:
1. \(\dfrac{5}{3}\) 2. \(\dfrac{5}{4}\)
3. \(\dfrac{3}{2}\) 4. \(\dfrac{4}{3}\)
questions.explanation:
Hint: \(R = \dfrac{L}{KA}\)

Step: Find the ratio \(\dfrac{T_1}{T_2}\).
For rods connected in series, the heat current is the same through each rod in the steady state. 
The net resistance of the rod is given by;
\(R_{net} = \dfrac{L}{2KA} + \dfrac{L}{KA} + \dfrac{L}{2KA} = \dfrac{2L}{KA}\)
Let \(\dfrac{L}{KA} = \alpha\)
\(R_{net} =2 \alpha\)
The current flow through the rod is given by;
\(i = \dfrac{3T-T}{2\alpha}= \dfrac{T}{\alpha}\)
At first junction, 
\( \dfrac{3T-T_1}{\dfrac{L}{2KA}}= \dfrac{T}{\alpha}\)
\(\Rightarrow \dfrac{3T-T_1}{\dfrac{\alpha }{2}}= \dfrac{T}{\alpha}\)
\(\Rightarrow {3T-T_1}= \dfrac{T}{2}\)
\(\Rightarrow T_1= 3T-\dfrac{T}{2} = \dfrac{5T}{2}~~~...(1)\)
At last junction, 
\( \dfrac{T_2-T}{\dfrac{L}{2KA}}= \dfrac{T}{\alpha}\)
\(\Rightarrow \dfrac{T_2-T}{\dfrac{\alpha }{2}}= \dfrac{T}{\alpha}\)
\(\Rightarrow {T_2-T}= \dfrac{T}{2} \)
\(\Rightarrow {T_2}= \dfrac{T}{2} + T = \dfrac{3T}{2}~~~...(2)\)
From equation \((1)\) and \((2)\) we get; 
\(\dfrac{T_1}{T_2} = \dfrac{5}{3}\)
Hence, option (1) is the correct answer.

questions.question:
In an oscillating spring mass system, a spring is connected to a box filled with the sand. As the box oscillates, sand leaks slowly out of the box vertically so that the average frequency \(\omega~(t)\) and average amplitude \(A~(t)\) of the system changes with time \(t.\) Which of the following options systemically depicts these changes correctly?
1. 2.
3. 4.
questions.explanation:
Hint: As sand leaks out, the system’s mass decreases causing frequency to rise

Explanation: When the sand leaks out, the mass of the box–spring system keeps decreasing, and because the frequency of a spring–mass system is \(\omega=\sqrt{k/m}, \) a smaller mass makes the frequency steadily increase with time. At the same time, each small amount of sand that falls off carries away some kinetic energy of the motion at the moment it detaches, so the system continuously loses mechanical energy. As a result, the amplitude of oscillation keeps decreasing with time. Thus, frequency rises while amplitude falls, which corresponds to option 4.
Hence, option (4) is the correct answer.

questions.question:
In some appropriate units, time \((t)\) and position \((x)\) relation of a moving particle is given by \(t=x^2+x. \) The acceleration of the particle is:
1. \(+\dfrac{2}{(x+1)^3}\) 2. \(+\dfrac{2}{(2x+1)}\)
3. \(-\dfrac{2}{(x+2)^3}\) 4. \(-\dfrac{2}{(2x+1)^3}\)
questions.explanation:
Hint: \(a=v\dfrac{dv}{dx}\)

Step 1: Find the velocity function.
\(t=x^2+x\)
\(\Rightarrow \dfrac{dt}{dx}=2x+1\)
\(\Rightarrow \dfrac{dx}{dt}=\dfrac{1}{2x+1}\)
\(\Rightarrow v=\dfrac{1}{2x+1}\)
Step 2: Find derivative of velocity function with respect to \(x.\)
\(v=(2x+1)^{-1}\)
\(\dfrac{dv}{dx}=-2(2x+1)^{-2}\)
\(\dfrac{dv}{dx}=-\dfrac{2}{(2x+1)^{2}}\)
Step 3: Find the acceleration of the particle.
\(a=v\dfrac{dv}{dx}\)
\(\Rightarrow a=-\dfrac{1}{2x+1}\times\dfrac{2}{(2x+1)^{2}}\)
\(\Rightarrow a=-\dfrac{2}{(2x+1)^{3}}\)
Hence, option (4) is the correct answer.

questions.question:
There are two inclined surfaces of equal length \((L)\) and same angle of inclination \(45^\circ\) with the horizontal. One of them is rough and the other is perfectly smooth. A given body takes \(2\) times as much time to slide down on rough surface than on the smooth surface. The coefficient of kinetic friction \((\mu_k)\) between the object and the rough surface is close to:
1. \(0.5\) 2. \(0.75\)
3. \(0.25\) 4. \(0.40\)
questions.explanation:
Explanation: 
\(\text{For motion down an inclined plane from rest, the time taken to cover distance is}\\ t=\sqrt{\frac{2 L}{a}} \\ \text{where a is the acceleration along the plane. For the smooth plane at }45^{\circ} :\\ a_s=g \sin 45^{\circ}=\frac{g}{\sqrt{2}} \)
\( a_s=g \sin 45^{\circ}=\frac{g}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \text{For the rough plane:}\\ a_r=g\left(\sin 45^{\circ}-\mu_k \cos 45^{\circ}\right)=\frac{g}{\sqrt{2}}\left(1-\mu_k\right)\\ \text{Given:}\\ t_r=2 t_s \\ \text{So,}\\ \sqrt{\frac{2 L}{a_r}}=2 \sqrt{\frac{2 L}{a_s}} \\ \text{Squaring:} \\ \frac{1}{a_r}=\frac{4}{a_s} \\ a_r=\frac{a_s}{4} \)
\( \begin{aligned} & \frac{1}{a_r}=\frac{4}{a_s} \\ & a_r=\frac{a_s}{4} \end{aligned} \\ \text{Substitute}: \\ \frac{g}{\sqrt{2}}\left(1-\mu_k\right)=\frac{1}{4} \cdot \frac{g}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \text{Cancel common terms: } \\ \begin{gathered} 1-\mu_k=\frac{1}{4} \\ \mu_k=\frac{3}{4}=0.75 \end{gathered} \)
Hence, option (2) is the correct answer.

Charge on each sphere is \(q\) and the force of repulsion between them is \(F. \) A third identical uncharged conducting sphere is brought in contact with sphere \(A\) first and then with \(B \) and finally removed from both. New force of repulsion between spheres \( A\) and \(B \) (Radii of \(A\) and \(B \) are negligible compared to the distance of separation so that for calculating force between them they can be considered as point charges) is best given as:

3. \(\dfrac{3 F}{5}\) 4. \(\dfrac{2 F}{3}\)

Hint: \(F=\dfrac{kq_1q_2}{r^2}\)

Step: Find the new  force of repulsion between spheres \( A\) and \(B .\)

questions.explanation:
Hint: \(2\pi r_n = n\lambda\)

Step: Find the de-Broglie wavelength of the electron orbiting in the state \(n=2\).
According to de-Broglie hypothesis, \(2\pi r_n = n\lambda~~~...(1)\)

\(r_n = n^2 a_0~~~...(2)\)

\(\Rightarrow \lambda = 2\pi n a_0\)
For \(n = 2\),
\(\Rightarrow \lambda = 4\pi a_0\)
\(\Rightarrow \lambda = 4\times 3.14 \times 0.052= 0.65312~\text{nm}\)
\(\Rightarrow \lambda \approx 0.67~\text{nm}\)
Hence, option (4) is the correct answer.

questions.question:
The correct order of decreasing basic strength of the given amines is:
1. N-ethylethanamine > ethanamine > N -methylaniline > benzenamine
2. benzenamine > ethanamine > N -methylaniline >N-ethylethanamine
3. N -methylaniline > benzenamine > ethanamine >N-ethylethanamine
4. N-ethylethanamine > ethanamine > benzenamine >N-methylaniline
questions.explanation:
​​​​​​​
 
  1. Ethanamine (C₂H₅NH₂):
    • This is a primary aliphatic amine.
    • The ethyl group is electron-donating via the inductive effect, increasing electron density on nitrogen, making it highly basic.
    • No resonance delocalization of the lone pair, so the lone pair is fully available for protonation.
  2. N-Ethylethanamine ((C₂H₅)₂NH):
    • This is a secondary aliphatic amine.
    • It has two ethyl groups, which provide a stronger inductive effect than in ethanamine, increasing electron density on nitrogen.
    • Secondary amines are often slightly more basic than primary amines due to the cumulative inductive effect, but solvation effects in aqueous solution can slightly reduce the difference.
    • In general, N-ethylethanamine is expected to be slightly more basic than ethanamine.
  3. Benzenamine (Aniline, C₆H₅NH₂):
    • This is a primary aromatic amine.
    • The nitrogen lone pair is delocalized into the benzene ring via resonance, reducing its availability for protonation.
    • Aromatic amines are significantly less basic than aliphatic amines due to this resonance effect.
    • The pKa of aniline’s conjugate acid is around 4.6, much lower than aliphatic amines (pKa ~10–11).
  4. N-Methylaniline (C₆H₅NHCH₃):
    • This is a secondary aromatic amine.
    • The methyl group on nitrogen provides a slight inductive electron-donating effect, which slightly increases the electron density on nitrogen compared to aniline.
    • However, the lone pair is still delocalized into the benzene ring, so it remains much less basic than aliphatic amines.
    • N-Methylaniline is generally slightly more basic than aniline due to the methyl group but far less basic than aliphatic amines.

General Trend:

  • Aliphatic amines (primary, secondary) are more basic than aromatic amines because their lone pairs are not delocalized.
  • Among aliphatic amines, secondary amines (like N-ethylethanamine) are slightly more basic than primary amines (like ethanamine) due to stronger inductive effects, though solvation can narrow this gap.
  • Among aromatic amines, N-methylaniline is slightly more basic than benzenamine (aniline) due to the electron-donating methyl group.
  • The basicity order is typically: secondary aliphatic > primary aliphatic > secondary aromatic > primary aromatic.

Which of the following statements are true for the ionization of phosphoric acid?
A. \(\log \mathrm{K}=\log \mathrm{K}_{\mathrm{a}_1}+\log \mathrm{K}_{\mathrm{a}_2}+\log \mathrm{K}_{\mathrm{a}_3}\)
B. \(\mathrm{H}_3 \mathrm{PO}_4\) is a stronger acid than \(\mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{PO}_4^{-}\) and \(\mathrm{HPO}_4^{2-} .\)
C. \(\mathrm{K}_{a_1} >\mathrm{~K}_{\mathrm{a}_2}>\mathrm{K}_{\mathrm{a}_3} \)
D. \(\mathrm{K}_{\mathrm{a}_1}=\frac{\mathrm{K}_{\mathrm{a}_3}+\mathrm{K}_{\mathrm{a}_2}}{2}\)
Choose the correct answer from the options given below : 
1. B, C and D only 
2. A, B and C only 
3. A and B only 
4. A and C only
questions.explanation:
Hint: \(\mathrm{K}_{a_1} >\mathrm{~K}_{\mathrm{a}_2}>\mathrm{K}_{\mathrm{a}_3} \)
 

Explanation:
(i) The overall ionization constant (K) is the product of the individual steps: \(K = K_{a_1} \times K_{a_2} \times K_{a_3}\), so on taking log on both sides we will get \(\log \mathrm{K}=\log \mathrm{K}_{\mathrm{a}_1}+\log \mathrm{K}_{\mathrm{a}_2}+\log \mathrm{K}_{\mathrm{a}_3}\) hence it is correct. 
(ii) \(\text{H}_3\text{PO}_4\) is a stronger acid than \(\text{H}_2\text{PO}_4^{-}\) and \(\text{HPO}_4^{2-}\).
(iii) The ionization constant decreases with each successive step. This is because it becomes more difficult to remove a positively charged proton \(\text{H}^+\) from an increasingly negatively charged anion, hence \(\mathrm{K}_{a_1} >\mathrm{~K}_{\mathrm{a}_2}>\mathrm{K}_{\mathrm{a}_3} \).
(iv) There is no general relationship that defines \(K_{a_1}\) as the arithmetic mean of \(K_{a_2}\) and \(K_{a_3}\).

Therefore, A,B, and C are correct.

questions.explanation:
Hint: Grignard reagent does nucleophilic addition. 
 
 

The Grignard reagent (\(CH_3MgBr\)) is a strong nucleophile. It first attacks the more reactive carbonyl group (ketone). Since it's in excess, it will fully convert the ketone into a tertiary alcohol after the final acidic workup (\(H_3O^+\)).

The excess Grignard then attacks the nitrile group.

  • One equivalent of \(CH_3MgBr\) adds to the \(C \equiv N\) triple bond to form an imine salt (specifically, a magnesium salt of an imine).

  • Normally, Grignard reagents can add twice to esters or acid chlorides to form alcohols, but they typically add only once to nitriles under these conditions because the resulting imine intermediate is negatively charged and resists further nucleophilic attack.

When \(H_3O^+\) is added in the second step:

  • The alkoxide formed at the original ketone site is protonated to an alcohol (-OH).

  • The imine salt at the nitrile site is hydrolyzed into a methyl ketone (\(-\text{C(=O)CH}_3\)).

This matches the structure in Option 4, which shows a tertiary alcohol on the left and a new methyl ketone on the right.
